name: room
text: Room opened — goal: Deliver: Push link coverage toward 100% at +5%/day (the access gate)

name: Reel
text: We should prioritize creating detailed, hands-on transcripts for our most frequently accessed content first. This approach will maximize our link coverage quickly and effectively, ensuring users gain immediate value from the most popular material. The trade-off here is that we may delay work on less accessed transcripts, but focusing on high-traffic areas allows us to achieve our coverage goal of 100% more efficiently.

name: Scriv
text: Scriv: Hold on—prioritizing *only* the most frequently accessed content risks leaving behind the *long-tail* of niche but critical links that still matter for compliance or edge cases. A better alternative is to split the work: first, a quick audit to flag *all* missing links (not just the popular ones), then tackle the high-impact ones first while scheduling the rest in a backlog. That way, we don’t trade one kind of risk for another. What would settle this? A concrete list of *all* missing links, ranked by both traffic *and* business need, so we’re not flying blind.

name: Chisel
text:
I think we should start with Scriv's suggested quick audit to flag all missing links, as this will give us a complete picture of the work that needs to be done. This approach may seem slower at first, but it's the best option for achieving our goal of 100% link coverage because it ensures we don't overlook critical niche links. By doing a thorough audit upfront, we're accepting the trade-off of a slightly slower initial progress, but we'll avoid the risk of leaving behind important links that could hinder our progress in the long run. This decision prioritizes quality and thoroughness, which aligns with our team's value of "quality first".
[dispatched 4 workers: worker-4987, worker-2745, worker-6149… — done, dissolved]

name: Sift
text: Sift: Hold on—starting with a full audit before touching *any* transcripts risks turning a 5%-per-day sprint into a weeks-long crawl. The real risk is that we’ll drown in data before we’ve earned a single new link. A better alternative is to run a lightweight scan that flags *only* the most glaring gaps (popular pages, compliance-heavy sections) while we simultaneously spin up a small team to tackle those first. That way, we hit the +5% daily target *and* avoid the paralysis of perfection. What would settle this? A 24-hour trial: audit the top 20% of pages by traffic, fix what’s broken there, and measure the coverage delta. If it stalls, we revisit the scope.
